They have linear growth and uniformly bounded spatial derivatives of orders one through six for $0\le s\le1$, because $D^jF$ is bounded for $1\le j\le6$. The O map is affine with centered Gaussian noise of uniformly bounded moments of every fixed order by [F2]. Differentiating these explicit maps and taking Gaussian expectations therefore shows that each $P_s^C$, $C\in\{A,B,O\}$, preserves bounds $|D^j\psi(z)|\le K_0W_r(z)$ through any stated order $k\le6$, uniformly for $s\le1$. Each generator maps such bounds through order $k$ to bounds through order $k-2$ with weight $W_{r+1}$: its drift coefficients grow at most linearly, their positive-order derivatives are bounded, and its second-order coefficients are constant. Thus a composition with at most three generator applications, even with subflow semigroups between them, uses at most six test derivatives and is bounded by $CW_{p+3}(z)$.

For any $r\ge0$, direct differentiation of $W_r$ and the linear-growth drift and constant diffusion give $|LW_r|\le C_rW_r$. Itô's formula [F3] stopped on a ball, the integral Gronwall estimate, and Fatou [F5] as the stopping radius increases give $P_uW_r(z)\le C_rW_r(z)$ for $0\le u\le1$. These are estimates from a fixed deterministic starting point; higher weights can be used to justify the localization limits. In particular, $|L^3\phi(z)|\le CW_{p+3}(z)$ by the same coefficient and derivative count as in step 1.1, and $|P_uL^3\phi(z)|\le CW_{p+3}(z)$. For the bounded-test branch this is the cubic weight $W_3$, using the same Lyapunov function with exponent $3/2$, not a higher initial-moment assumption.
